recent_posts.title: PyCoder’s Weekly
recent_posts.summary: PyCoder's Weekly Issue #733 covers a range of Python ecosystem news and tutorials. Highlights include a podcast on agentic data science with marimo pair, using LLMs to find Python C-extension bugs, and a one-month retrospective on httpxyz (a fork of httpx). Notable Python news includes PyPy v7.3.22 release, acceptance of several PEPs (661 sentinel values, 831 frame pointers, 820 PySlot, 829 site.toml config), pip 26.1 new features including dependency cooldowns and pylock.toml support, and the approval of the Python Packaging Council. Articles cover async task queues, Python logging library comparisons (logging vs structlog vs Loguru), Django project redesign, and AI coding agent workflow types. Projects section features cadquery, secure HTTP headers library, a Rust-based Jest-style test runner, and more.

recent_posts.title: Word counter that ignores Markdown
recent_posts.summary: A Python CLI tool that counts words in Markdown files by stripping Markdown syntax using regular expressions before counting. The script uses typer and rich for the CLI interface, supports single files or directories, and provides verbose stats including word count, lines, characters, sentences, average word length, and estimated reading time. The author shares their love of regular expressions as the motivation for building this instead of using a Markdown rendering library.

recent_posts.title: Python __getitem__, __getattr__, __getattribute__ and __get__ explained
recent_posts.summary: A deep dive into Python's four 'get' dunder methods: `__getitem__`, `__getattr__`, `__getattribute__`, and `__get__`. Explains how `__getitem__` handles square bracket subscript access, while the other three deal with dot notation. Clarifies that `__getattribute__` is called on every attribute access via dot notation, while `__getattr__` serves as a fallback only when the attribute isn't found through normal routes. Also covers the descriptor protocol, explaining the priority order `__getattribute__` uses: data descriptors first, then instance attributes, then non-data descriptors, then class attributes, and finally `__getattr__` as a last resort.

recent_posts.title: Introducing Apache Arrow Support in mssql-python
recent_posts.summary: mssql-python now supports fetching SQL Server data directly as Apache Arrow structures, enabling zero-copy, columnar data transfer to Polars, Pandas, DuckDB, and other Arrow-native libraries. Three new Cursor APIs are introduced: cursor.arrow_batch() for incremental batch fetching, cursor.arrow() for eager full result set retrieval as a pyarrow.Table, and cursor.arrow_reader() for lazy streaming via a RecordBatchReader. The Arrow path avoids Python object creation per row, reducing GC pressure and memory usage. Temporal types like DATETIME and DATETIMEOFFSET show the largest performance gains since timezone normalization runs entirely in C++. A known limitation exists for NVARCHAR on Linux due to a slower UTF-16 to UTF-8 conversion path, with a fix planned. The feature was contributed by community developer Felix Graßl and is purely additive — existing fetchone/fetchmany/fetchall code is unaffected.

recent_posts.title: Asking the Key Questions: Q&A with the PyCon US 2026 keynote speaker Pablo Galindo Salgado
recent_posts.summary: Pablo Galindo Salgado, a Python core developer and PyCon US 2026 keynote speaker, shares his journey into tech through Physics simulations, his most meaningful contributions (including the PEG parser, error messages, and mentoring new contributors), and advice for first-time conference attendees. He emphasizes the human side of CPython development, encouraging developers to demystify the project and consider contributing, noting that core developers are ordinary people doing collaborative, imperfect work in the open.

recent_posts.title: Asking the Key Questions: Q&A with the PyCon US 2026 keynote speaker amanda casari
recent_posts.summary: A Q&A interview with amanda casari, a keynote speaker at PyCon US 2026. She shares her journey into Python starting in 2009, her involvement with PyLadies Seattle, her focus on making space for hope in open source, and tips for first-time conference attendees. She also highlights RTEMS, a 30-year-old open source real-time operating system used in space missions, as an underappreciated project.

recent_posts.title: TIL #144 – Sentinel built-in
recent_posts.summary: Python 3.15 introduces a new built-in `sentinel()` function for creating sentinel values. Previously, developers used `object()` as a workaround, but this approach and other common sentinel idioms have known shortcomings. PEP 661 documents the motivation behind the new built-in and the problems it solves.

recent_posts.title: Inverse Sapir-Whorf and programming languages
recent_posts.summary: An exploration of the 'Inverse Sapir-Whorf' concept applied to programming languages — the idea that languages force you to express things you may not care about. Drawing parallels from natural language (English gendered pronouns, Turkish evidential tenses), the post examines how programming languages compel programmers to specify evaluation order, async/sync function coloring, memory allocation, variable scope, and types, even when those details are irrelevant to the programmer's intent. Gradually typed languages are highlighted as one approach that reduces this forced expression.

recent_posts.title: Tryton News May 2026
recent_posts.summary: Tryton's May 2026 newsletter covers recent improvements building on the LTS 8.0 release. Key changes include updating Stripe API support to version 2026-03-25.dahlia, including timesheet costs in production work costs, adding a URL fallback on model name, supporting email sending and replies from chat messages, moving several accounting modules to the external tryton-community project, adding new REST API documentation, and releasing bug fixes for LTS series 8.0, 7.0, 6.0 as well as 7.8 and 7.6. Developers also benefit from a fallback to compact RelaxNG syntax when files are not present.

recent_posts.title: Connect Streamlit buttons to trigger actions
recent_posts.summary: A beginner-friendly guide to using buttons in Streamlit to add interactivity to Python web apps. Covers the basic st.button() syntax, handling multiple buttons with different actions, displaying dynamic content (text, images) based on button clicks, creating dynamic forms triggered by buttons, and grouping inputs with st.form() for batch submission. Also explains Streamlit's stateless execution model and why button state doesn't persist between interactions.
